nameStory: The 'salted' part of this lichen's name comes from the tiny white granules scattered across its surface that look just like coarse salt crystals sprinkled on food. The 'ruffle' refers to its wavy, leaf-like lobes that fold and ripple like fabric ruffles or lettuce leaves. It's a perfect name that captures both the texture you'll feel and the distinctive white specks you'll see!
description: Salted ruffle lichen is a leafy, gray-green lichen that grows flat against tree bark in overlapping, wavy lobes. Each lobe can spread 2-4 inches across, with the whole colony sometimes reaching dinner-plate size on large trees. Its most distinctive feature is the scattered white, salt-like granules (called soredia) that dust the surface, especially toward the center. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together: a fungus and an algae working as partners.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for tiny white granules scattered across the surface that feel gritty like coarse salt when you gently rub them with your finger. These powdery spots are most noticeable in the center of the lichen.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leafy lobes that wave and ruffle at the edges like lettuce leaves. The lobes overlap each other and attach to bark at multiple points, not just the center.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green on top when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet from rain or morning dew. The underside is black with white patches near the edges.

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found on tree bark, particularly favoring hardwoods like oak and maple. Rarely seen on rocks or other surfaces.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes can reach 2-4 inches across, with mature colonies sometimes spanning 8-12 inches on large tree trunks.

habitat: Look for salted ruffle lichen on the bark of mature hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, especially oaks and maples. It prefers areas with good air quality and moderate humidity, so you're more likely to find it in established forests rather than along busy roadsides. It grows from sea level up to mid-elevations in the mountains.

seasonality.spring: The white salt-like granules are most visible as the lichen becomes active with spring moisture. Colors appear more vibrant green after spring rains.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer periods, the lichen appears gray and somewhat shriveled, but the distinctive white granules remain visible. Early morning dew may temporarily green it up.
seasonality.fall: Fall rains rejuvenate the lichen, making it plump and green again. This is an excellent time to see the contrast between the vibrant surface and dark undersides.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible on trees but appears dormant and gray. Snow and ice may highlight the ruffle-like edges, and the white granules still provide identification clues.

funFact: Those salt-like granules aren't just for show – they're actually tiny survival packages containing both fungal threads and algae cells that can blow away in the wind to start new lichen colonies elsewhere, making each speck a potential new organism!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with other ruffle lichens in the same genus, but the distinctive white granules scattered across the surface are your key clue – they look exactly like someone sprinkled coarse salt on the lichen. If you don't see these gritty white specks, you're probably looking at a different ruffle lichen species.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name has changed over time – it was originally called Parmelia crinita when first described in 1814, but was moved to the genus Parmotrema in 1952 as scientists better understood lichen relationships. Don't be confused if you see it listed under the old name in older field guides.
compareHints: Salted ruffle lichen stands out from its ruffle lichen relatives by those distinctive white, salt-like granules scattered across its surface. Other ruffle lichens in New England might have holes (perforated ruffle), white powder in patches (powdered ruffle), or smooth surfaces, but none have that distinctive 'salted' appearance. The granules are your best identification feature – no other ruffle lichen has quite the same gritty, salt-crystal texture.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike perforated ruffle lichen which has distinctive holes, powdered ruffle lichen has a continuous surface covered in soredia.
Unlike its powdered ruffle lichen cousin which has a dusty, powdery surface, perforated ruffle lichen has a smooth surface and those unmistakable perforated fruiting bodies.

Unlike its relatives the Perforated Ruffle Lichen (which has distinctive holes) or the Powdered Ruffle Lichen (which has a dusty, powdery surface), Black Sheet Lichen has a smooth, unperforated surface.
